Norm for a finite free ring extension (NB/A​(b)=det(mb​))

Words: 60
Commutative algebra OurBigBook.com
If B is a commutative A-algebra which is a finite free module over A, its norm sends b to the determinant of multiplication mb​:B→B. The determinant is independent of the chosen basis and is multiplicative because mbc​=mb​mc​. It commutes with scalar extension. On a separable field extension it becomes the product over embeddings, recovering the field norm. An invertible b has invertible norm.

Finite-type integer algebra (R=Z[r1​,…,rm​])

Words: 121 Articles: 1
Commutative algebra OurBigBook.com
A unital commutative ring generated by finitely many elements under addition and multiplication, starting from the image of the integers. Equivalently it is a quotient of a finite-variable polynomial ring over Z. localization of a ring at one element remains finite type, since R[1/r]≅R[T]/(rT−1). Generation here is as an algebra, not merely as a field extension when the ring happens to be a field.

Finite-field theorem for finitely generated integer algebras

Words: 63
Finite-type integer algebra OurBigBook.com
A field that is a finite-type integer algebra has prime characteristic or zero. Prime characteristic and Zariski lemma make it a finite algebraic extension of a finite prime field. In characteristic zero, the same lemma makes it a number field; clearing finitely many coefficient denominators makes it integral over Z[1/N]. The integral field extension forces the base domain to be a field, but a prime not dividing N is not invertible there. This contradiction excludes characteristic zero.

Valuation ring OurBigBook.com
A valuation ring for a nontrivial real-valued rank-one valuation is a principal ideal domain exactly when its value group is discrete. A least positive value makes the value group cyclic and lets every nonzero ideal be generated by an element of smallest valuation. Conversely, if the maximal ideal is principal, its generator has the least positive value. Nontriviality matters: a field with the trivial valuation is a principal ideal domain, but not a discrete valuation ring in the usual nontrivial convention.

Valuation ring OurBigBook.com
Every local subring A of a field K is dominated by a valuation ring with fraction field K. Order local overrings by inclusion and contraction of their maximal ideals; chain unions are local, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal one. For each z∈K×, at least one of the extensions of its maximal ideal to V[z] and V[z−1] is proper: otherwise two least-degree relations for 1 with maximal-ideal coefficients reduce one another to a smaller-degree relation. Localizing the proper extension gives a dominating overring, so maximality forces either z or z−1 into V.

A subsequence map f has f(k)≥k, so containment of the matched later slice implies containment of the slice at k; the final-slice comparison handles the tail. Multiplicativity of the nonarchimedean polynomial norm (∥fg∥G​=∥f∥G​∥g∥G​)
Words: 79
Gauss lemma for polynomials OurBigBook.com
For a field with a Non-Archimedean absolute value, define the coefficient norm ∥f∥G​=maxi​∣ai​∣ for f(T)=∑i​ai​Ti. Then ∥fg∥G​=∥f∥G​∥g∥G​. For nonzero polynomials, scale each by one of its coefficients of maximum absolute value; the resulting polynomials have integral coefficients and at least one unit coefficient. Their reductions in the residue field are nonzero, so their product is nonzero. The product therefore also has coefficient norm 1, proving the formula after reversing the scaling. This compares binary-polynomial coefficient heights with the heights of their roots.
Polynomial ring over a unique factorization domain
Words: 112 Articles: 1
Gauss lemma for polynomials OurBigBook.com
If R is a unique factorization domain with fraction field F, then R[X] is a unique factorization domain. A primitive polynomial irreducible in R[X] remains irreducible, hence prime, in the principal ideal domain F[X]; Gauss lemma for polynomials brings divisibility back to R[X].
Integer polynomial ring is not a principal ideal domain (Z[X])
Words: 73
Polynomial ring over a unique factorization domain OurBigBook.com
The polynomial ring Z[X] is a unique factorization domain by Gauss lemma for polynomials, but its ideal (2,X) is not principal. Any generator would divide both 2 and X, hence be a unit: a divisor of 2 has degree zero, and a constant dividing X is ±1. Yet evaluation at zero followed by reduction modulo 2 annihilates the ideal and not 1. It embeds in the principal ideal domain Q[X], illustrating that the property need not pass to a subring.
Symmetric rational function in two variables
Words: 52
Gauss lemma for polynomials OurBigBook.com
Every rational function in C(X,Y) fixed by exchanging X and Y is a quotient of coprime symmetric polynomials. In a coprime presentation p/q, symmetry gives
pq∗=p∗q.
(38)
Unique factorization implies p∗=λp and q∗=λq. The alternative λ=−1 would make both divisible by X−Y, contradicting coprimality, so λ=1.

Eisenstein criterion

Words: 155 Articles: 2
Commutative algebra OurBigBook.com
For a primitive polynomial
F(X)=an​Xn+⋯+a0​∈Z[X],
(39)
if a prime p does not divide an​, divides every aj​ for j<n, and has p2∤a0​, then F is irreducible. If F=GH, reduction modulo p forces both G and H to be positive-degree monomials. Their constant terms are consequently divisible by p, making p2∣F(0), a contradiction. Gauss lemma for polynomials transfers the result between Z[X] and Q[X].

(p)=Pn,vP​(α)=1.

This conclusion concerns the full ring of integers of a number field and does not assume that it equals Z[α].

Odd-valuation obstruction to a rational-function square

Words: 44
Commutative algebra OurBigBook.com
Every zero and pole of a square in K(Y) has even order. Thus a rational function with a zero or pole of odd order cannot be a square. For characteristic different from two, this proves that 1−Y2 is not a square in K(Y).

Minimal prime ideal

Words: 176 Articles: 3
Prime ideal OurBigBook.com
A minimal prime ideal is a prime ideal containing no strictly smaller prime ideal. If A is a reduced ring and p is minimal, the localization at a prime ideal Ap​ is a field: its only prime is its maximal ideal, and reducedness makes that ideal its zero nilradical. Every nonzero commutative ring has a minimal prime.

Minimal prime over an ideal (P∈MinR​(I))

Words: 23
Minimal prime ideal OurBigBook.com
A prime ideal P is minimal over an ideal I if I⊆P and no smaller prime ideal contains I. The definition also applies to two-sided prime ideals of a noncommutative ring.

Existence of minimal primes over a proper ideal (MinR​(I)=∅)

Words: 46
Minimal prime ideal OurBigBook.com
Every proper ideal of a unital commutative ring is contained in a minimal prime over that ideal. A maximal ideal supplies a prime containing it, and an intersection of a decreasing chain of primes is still prime. Zorn's lemma, with reverse inclusion, therefore supplies a minimal member. No Noetherian assumption is needed.

Unique minimal prime does not imply primary

Words: 57
Minimal prime ideal OurBigBook.com
In k[u,v], the ideal I=(u2,uv) has radical of an ideal (u), a prime ideal, and hence a unique minimal prime ideal. Nevertheless uv∈I, u∈/I, and vj∈/I for all j≥1, so I is not a primary ideal. The same example works after adjoining inverses of 1+u and 1+v; thus it also gives an example in a two-variable Laurent polynomial ring.

Prime ideal avoiding a multiplicative subset

Words: 86
Prime ideal OurBigBook.com
In a Noetherian ring, an ideal I disjoint from a nonempty multiplicative subset S extends to an ideal P maximal among those disjoint from S, by the ascending chain condition. It is proper. If ab∈P but neither factor belongs to P, both P+(a) and P+(b) meet S. Multiplying such representatives puts an element of S in P, a contradiction. Thus P is a prime ideal. For a general commutative ring the same argument follows after applying the Zorn lemma to disjoint ideals; the union of a chain is disjoint from S.

The nth symbolic power of a prime ideal P⊂R is
P(n)=PnRP​∩R,
(42)
where the intersection denotes contraction of an ideal. It is always a P-primary ideal. The ordinary power Pn equals P(n) precisely when Pn is P-primary; this assertion does not require R to be Noetherian.

Prime ideal quotient criterion

Prime ideal OurBigBook.com
For a commutative unital ring R, an ideal I is prime exactly when R/I is an integral domain. The zero-product condition in the quotient translates directly to ab∈I.

A nonzero Boolean integral domain has only the elements zero and one, so it is F2​. The quotient criterion then makes every prime quotient of a Boolean ring a field, and every prime ideal maximal.
